title: The Genius of Airplane!: How to Make a Comedy by Playing Everything Completely Straight
description:
in Comedy, Film |   	August 17th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Not every 46-year-old com­e­dy still gets laughs, but Air­plane! seems only to get
body:
in Comedy, Film |   	August 17th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Not every 46-year-old com­e­dy still gets laughs, but Air­plane! seems only to get fun­nier with the decades. Some view­ers too young to have caught it in its the­atri­cal release even take the Ben­jamin­ian view of it as the kind of great work that cre­ates its own genre: the rapid-fire dead­pan joke machine, we could call it. But as the InCin­e­mat­ic video essay above reminds us, Air­plane! belongs, at its core, to that ven­er­a­ble comedic form of the par­o­dy. The key lies in its tit­u­lar excla­ma­tion point shared with Zero Hour!, a con­ven­tion­al Para­mount dis­as­ter movie from 1957 also about a dis­graced fight­er pilot forced to assume com­mand of an air­lin­er, albeit one with nary a laugh in its 81 min­utes.
Though it actu­al­ly runs six min­utes longer, Air­plane! feels much short­er, thanks in part to its mer­ci­less­ly con­stant vol­ley of humor. But unlike so many major par­o­dies of this cen­tu­ry, which feel like noth­ing so much as a tis­sue of rapid­ly expir­ing pop-cul­ture ref­er­ences, it also tells a gen­uine sto­ry with momen­tum of its own.
The film’s writer-direc­to­r­i­al trio of Jim Abra­hams, David Zuck­er, and Jer­ry Zuck­er under­stood that view­ers would come for the laughs, but as with Zero Hour! and the count­less oth­er dis­as­ter pic­tures at which Air­plane! pokes fun, they’d stay to find out what hap­pens. Hence the inspired choice to play the whole thing per­fect­ly straight, no mat­ter how groan-induc­ing the visu­al or ver­bal gags being deliv­ered.
All this works only because Abra­hams, Zuck­er, and Zuck­er cast the right actors: that is to say, non-fun­ny ones. At the time of Air­plane!‘s release, “most come­dies relied on actors to be fun­ny, but nobody had real­ly tried mak­ing a com­e­dy with­out come­di­ans before.” This meant that “the com­e­dy had to be there before the cam­era start­ed rolling,” so that the actors being seem­ing­ly unaware of the humor would only make it fun­nier. The per­son­i­fi­ca­tion of this method is, of course, Leslie Nielsen, who’d already put in a quar­ter-cen­tu­ry of dra­mat­ic per­for­mances (includ­ing in no less a sev­en­ties dis­as­ter spec­ta­cle than The Posei­don Adven­ture), but whose dead­pan turn as Dr. Rumack ele­vat­ed him into a kind of super­star­dom of the absurd. Whether a par­o­dy like Air­plane! would work if made today is dif­fi­cult to say, but it nev­er­the­less remains a les­son in sto­ry­telling for young film­mak­ers — comedic or oth­er­wise.
Relat­ed Con­tent:
Sein­feld, Louis C.K., Chris Rock, and Ricky Ger­vais Dis­sect the Craft of Com­e­dy (NSFW)
Buster Keaton: The Won­der­ful Gags of the Found­ing Father of Visu­al Com­e­dy
Why Is Jack­ie Chan the King of Action Com­e­dy? A Video Essay Mas­ter­ful­ly Makes the Case
The Air­line Toi­lets The­atre Com­pa­ny: Watch One Man Stage Com­i­cal Shows in Air­plane Bath­rooms
Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: The Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam Has Digitized 840,000 Works of Art, Including Great Works by Rembrandt and Vermeer
description:
in Art |   	August 17th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Art may seem inessen­tial to those who make the big deci­sions in times of cri­sis. But it nev­
body:
in Art |   	August 17th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Art may seem inessen­tial to those who make the big deci­sions in times of cri­sis. But it nev­er seemed more nec­es­sary to artists work­ing in the time of plague. So it was 366 years ago when Rem­brandt paint­ed a por­trait of his son, Titus, in a monk’s robe in 1660. Eight years lat­er, Titus was dead from plague, which had only a few years ear­li­er killed Hen­drick­je Stof­fels, Rembrandt’s for­mer house­keep­er and sec­ond wife, who helped raise Titus, Rembrandt’s only child to sur­vive into adult­hood.
These unimag­in­able loss­es “con­tributed to the tragedy and anguish we see in Rem­brandt’s late self-por­traits,” writes The Guardian’s Jonathan Jones. Dur­ing the plague, Rem­brandt also used his work as social cri­tique.
His etch­ing The Rat-Poi­son Ped­dler shows, “in a sense,” the Min­neapo­lis Insti­tute of Art’s Tom Rassieur tells the Star Tri­bune, “the guy who pur­ports to be helping—the exterminator—is prob­a­bly doing as much to spread the dis­ease as any­one else. That relates to [crit­i­cism] of our lead­er­ship today.” In his last years, Rem­brandt paint­ed self-por­traits of his iso­la­tion and grief that found a new audi­ence dur­ing the COVID lock­down.

Else­where in the Nether­lands, Rembrandt’s con­tem­po­rary Johannes Ver­meer was no stranger to the kind of social­ly iso­lat­ed world we found our­selves in dur­ing COVID. “His home­town of Delft was strick­en with plague sev­er­al times in the artist’s life­time. In 1635 and 1636 over 2,000 peo­ple died, and in the mid-1650s and mid-1660s hun­dreds more,” notes Breeze Bar­ring­ton at CNN. The qual­i­ties we most asso­ciate with Vermeer’s work, the soli­tude and atten­tive pres­ence, were devel­oped dur­ing time spent in iso­la­tion.
“In this time of forced iso­la­tion,” Friso Lam­mertse, cura­tor of 17th-cen­tu­ry Dutch paint­ing at the Rijksmu­se­um in Ams­ter­dam, not­ed dur­ing the pan­dem­ic, Vermeer’s work “can point us at the fact that extreme beau­ty can be found just in our room.” The Rijksmu­se­um did­n’t just rec­om­mend art in the pan­demic’s state of alone­ness, but also dou­bled its col­lec­tion of free, high-res­o­lu­tion works online, by Rem­brandt, Ver­meer, and a host of oth­er artists who used art to cope with loss and lone­li­ness dur­ing the plagues of their times. The muse­um now offers 840,000 dig­i­tized images in total.
The muse­um promised to “bring the muse­um to you,” and it has deliv­ered not only with its exten­sive dig­i­tal col­lec­tion, free for down­load­ing, shar­ing and edit­ing with a free Rijksmu­se­um account, but also with infor­ma­tive series on its web­site. Art is essen­tial in the best and worst of times, when it shows us how to look close­ly at our­selves, our loved ones, and our sur­round­ings, and treat life with more care and atten­tion. Enter the Rijksmu­se­um online col­lec­tions here.
An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2021.
Relat­ed Con­tent: 
Rijksmu­se­um Dig­i­tizes & Makes Free Online 361,000 Works of Art, Mas­ter­pieces by Rem­brandt Includ­ed!
Explore the New 717-Gigapix­el Scan of Rembrandt’s The Night Watch, the Most Detailed Pho­to Ever Tak­en of a Work of Art
See the Com­plete Works of Ver­meer in Aug­ment­ed Real­i­ty: Google Makes Them Avail­able on Your Smart­phone
Josh Jones is a writer and musi­cian based in Durham, NC.

title: Clay Transforms into Vibrant and Funky 'Habibti' Sculptures by Maryam Yousif
description: Inspired by both the 20th-century funk art movement in the Bay Area and the visual language of the country of her birth, Iraqi-American artist Mar
body:
Inspired by both the 20th-century funk art movement in the Bay Area and the visual language of the country of her birth, Iraqi-American artist Maryam Yousif merges ancient cultural heritage and contemporary playfulness in vibrant ceramics. Born in Baghdad, she immigrated to the U.S. when she was young and is currently based in San Francisco.
Over the past several years, Yousif has developed her signature Habibti figures, which encapsulate the Arabic endearment for “sweetheart” or “darling,” each adorned with a dress of flowers, landscapes, and other shapes. Many of the works shown here were recently on view in the artist’s solo exhibition at The Pit titled Above Earth, Under The Rays of the Sun, which took its title from a curse tablet uncovered in the Assyrian queens’ tombs in the ancient city of Nimrud.

Few materials are as timeless and versatile as clay, which has been used to make pottery and other objects for thousands of years. Just last year, a 3,000-year-old pottery workshop was unearthed by archaeologists in an Iron Age settlement in Iraq. “Clay, as a medium, has a way of connecting us to the past, and in using it, it opened an interest into historical research,” Yousif tells Colossal. “It’s been so rewarding to study ancient objects, learn how to distill what I’m looking at into new ideas, and create my own world and mythology.” 
The artist describes how she’s compelled to follow rabbit holes in her research, from supernatural beings to queens and their gravesites to industry and commerce. She’s particularly interested in the nature of objects as symbolic or representative of places. Having left her first home for an entirely new experience in a different culture, she explores what it means to bring things with us or, indeed, leave them behind.
“Most of the research I’ve delved into takes place in and around Mesopotamia, too, which I’m always curious about since it’s linked to my background and home country of Iraq,” Yousif says. “I feel like working this way keeps me metaphysically connected to a place that I feel essentially far from in many ways.”
Yousif is currently working toward another solo exhibition with Rebecca Camacho Presents in San Francisco, slated for January. A commissioned work titled “Midrib” will also be included in the exhibition Ancient Queenship: Art, Power, and Presence at the Getty Villa starting in February.

title: Deepen Your Creative Practice at Vermont Studio Center
description:
Announcement
                 Full and partial fellowships available for artists and writers
body:
Announcement
                 Full and partial fellowships available for artists and writers
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
    
        
            A Vermont Studio Center residency provides artists and writers from around the world with the time and space to deepen their creative practice while building a solid network of mentors, collaborators, and friends. Sessions run for two, three, and four weeks, and include resident presentations, open studios, and an acclaimed Visiting Artists & Writers program. Nestled in the Green Mountains, Vermont Studio Center hosts a global community within a historic, pastoral village. The walkable campus provides private studios, a dining hall, and private rooms in shared lodging along the banks of the Gihon River. Residents can explore swimming holes, hiking and biking trails, and the rural charm of neighboring towns as they expand their creative potential and build a creative community.The fall 2026 open call runs from August 15 through September 30 and will fill residencies from July 2027 to December 2027. Each session welcomes 40 residents of varying mediums and genres at all career levels. All residents receive partial fellowships and 35% receive full fellowships.  Learn more at vermontstudiocenter.org

title: Chris Kraus, Relational, and the Moon
description:
Daily Newsletter
                The acclaimed writer sits down with artists Shirley Tse and Dana Berman Duff for a dialogue on
body:
Daily Newsletter
                The acclaimed writer sits down with artists Shirley Tse and Dana Berman Duff for a dialogue on breath, the universe, and the ephemeral forces that carry us.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            You may know Chris Kraus for her 1997 epistolary novel I Love Dick and other cult classics, or for her experimental films and incisive cultural criticism. For the last two decades, she has also followed and written about the work of Shirley Tse and Dana Berman Duff, and after reading Kraus’s interview with the artists — who collaborate under the name “Relational” — it’s plain to see why their work had such a pull on the writer. Lunar power and tidal waves are among the elements of their video-photo-sculptural exhibition The Universe Breathes Us, a poetic manifesto on the ephemeral forces that carry us.Speaking of unseen energies, artist Lauren Farkas's whimsical maps trace Knoxville, Tennessee's art ecosystem in felt, wire, animation, and watercolor. Also today, Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar on a new digital archive rooted in oral histories that honors the journalists killed in the Gaza genocide. —Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

	
		
		Shirley Tse and Dana Berman Duff’s Breathing Moons
		
	
	
		When sculptor Shirley Tse was invited by her former student Anna Hrund Másdóttir to produce an original exhibition at her cooperative gallery King and Bang in Reykjavik, her first thought was to invite her friend and former teacher, the film and video maker Dana Berman Duff, to collaborate with her. 
      
Geography, landscape, desire and time are some of the interests these two artists shared. The result is an extraordinary manifestation of physical elements — breath, moon and tides — that bind us and the universe. 
        
Working under the name “Relational,” their exhibition The Universe Breathes Us was exhibited at Kling and Bang in 2025, and again this summer at Shoshana Wayne Gallery in Los Angeles. Both iterations included a live choral performance of an original song by Berman Duff and her husband, the composer-musician Alan Duff Berman. Seeing it for the first time, I was struck by the deceptive simplicity of each of the elements and the subtly seamless ways that they animate each other. | Chris Kraus
	
	
		Read More
	

NewsA new archive developed by Writers Against the War on Gaza serves as a digital memorial for the Palestinian journalists killed in Gaza since October 2023. An 11-year-old boy sets the Guinness Record for the World's Youngest Curator after opening the Cambridge Natural History Museum in Illinois.Feature

Bravo! to Brian Karl's assessment of the Hammer exhibition. In this contemporary world of obsessive devotion to ancestors (real or imagined) it is refreshing to learn that some artist's efforts do fail to visually communicate. The inclusion of Mary Sully's is a significant plus. This under-rated work of portraiture, though humble in physical presence, stands as a monument of incisive creativity that speaks of indigenous backgrounds while simultaneously addressing contemporary culture. Such grand visual thinking!—Don Dugal on "The Living World Feels Dead at the Hammer"From the Archive

title: Bryan Joseph Lee Named Deputy Commissioner of New York City Cultural Affairs
description: The New York City Department of Cultural Affairs (DCLA) has named two senior leadership appointments: Bryan Joseph Lee as deputy commissioner and Ry
body:
The New York City Department of Cultural Affairs (DCLA) has named two senior leadership appointments: Bryan Joseph Lee as deputy commissioner and Ryan Max as chief of staff.

	Their appointments, according to a release, “will help guide the agency as it rolls out ambitious new programs to deliver on the Mamdani administration’s affordability agenda for the cultural community, while focusing in supporting the work of agency staff to deliver excellence in public service.”

	Lee is a cultural strategist and producer, who since 2021 has a Harlem-based consultancy named CNTR ARTS. His two-decade career has spanned working in the performing arts and museums, and his clients have included the National Endowment for the Arts, the Mid-America Artist Alliance, the Mellon Foundation, and the Wallace Foundation. Previously he served as the artistic director of the Public Forum at the Public Theater. During his tenure at Public Forum, he produced over 75 programs featuring over 250 artists. He has also independently produced programs at Lincoln Center, La MaMa, and the Shed.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	“In a time when the city is looking for leadership that can boost, ground, and galvanize the support that is needed, I am ecstatic to see Bryan Joseph Lee join this forward thinking administration,” Jonathan McCory, executive artistic director of the National Black Theater in Harlem, said in a statement.“He has worked in the sector for years and seen how each neighborhood has been affected by, supported, and deserves creative opportunities focused on providing access to all.”

	Since 2014, Max has been the department’s director of external affairs, where he has overseen the communications strategy for the county’s largest municipal funder of the arts. During his tenure, he has led the public roll-out for several of the department’s initiatives, including IDNYC cultural benefit program and its response to the pandemic’s effect on the cultural sector.

	In a statement, former commissioner Tom Finkelpearl said, “Ryan Max has earned the trust and respect of colleagues across the agency, city government and the cultural community. As Chief of Staff, Ryan will bring integrity, humanity and strategic vision to this essential role in the agency.”
	

	In a statement, DCLA commissioner Diya Vij described Max as “a pillar of every major initiative to come out of DCLA since 2014” and Lee as a cultural worker who has “spent years pushing for greater equity and care for artists and workers.”

	She added, “Lee brings a depth of experience across the performing arts, shaping grant programs, building the capacity of nonprofits, curating groundbreaking performances and festivals, and leading major community engagement initiatives. … Ryan will be instrumental to DCLA’s ability to execute an excellence in government that this administration strives for.”

title: Why Brancusi’s Sleek, Streamlined Sculptures Still Seduce
description:
“The legendary actress visits Christie’s galleries at Rockefeller Center and finds herself captivated by the gilded sculpture.” 

	Thus trumpets the
body:
“The legendary actress visits Christie’s galleries at Rockefeller Center and finds herself captivated by the gilded sculpture.” 

	Thus trumpets the tagline for Nicole Kidman’s assignation with Constantin Brancusi’s bronze and gold leaf Danaïde (1913), circulated online this past spring in advance of the work’s auction.  The “cinematic short film” produced by Christie’s indeed reveals the Hollywood star finding herself… duly captivated.

	She rushes an unnamed caller off the phone to stalk the sculpture in her stilettos from behind a circular curtain. To the tune of David Bowie’s “Golden Years,” Kidman gazes fixedly into Danaïde’s burnished, nearly vacant visage. The camera cuts intermittently to a speculative montage of her inner experience. 
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Like some ancient oracle, the sculpture’s mere presence unleashes a series of visionary insights into its presumed (read: decidedly fantastical) origins: from all manner of Greek statuary to eastern Buddhas, from the latter-day pre-Raphaelite painting The Danaïdes (1904) by John William Waterhouse to (utterly anachronistically) Alberto Giacometti’s 1951 sculpture The Chariot (Does Christie’s not employ a single art historian among its marketing ranks?). 

	Stare into the abyss and the abyss stares back. Or so Kidman’s filmed epiphany would suggest. She ends up dancing around the sculpture with tousled hair like some latter-day, midtown Maenad, her face—and ostensibly her soul—convulsed by the sculpture’s extrasensory revelations. 

	Danaïde left the block for a record $107.6 million, breaking the record for the auctioned sale of a sculpture. Whether Kidman’s performance inched the price upward remains unclear. It nevertheless undeniably played into a moment of renewed attention to the artist.


			
			
			
	
			
					View of the 2026 exhibition “Brancusi” at the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin. 
									Photo David von Becker. ©Succession Brancusi/VG Bild-Kunst
	



	BEFORE HIS DEATH in Paris at the age of 81, the Romanian-born Brancusi (1876–1957) bequeathed his estate to the French government on one condition: that his 15th arrondissement studio be reconstructed and preserved in perpetuity. Ongoing renovations of the Centre Pompidou, which has long since hosted the “Atelier Brancusi” in its abutting plaza, have set the workspace and its wide-ranging contents on the road. 
	

	They landed this summer at Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie, the first major exhibition of Brancusi’s work in Germany for a half century. MoMA will mount its own version of the show in October. More than 150 sculptures—along with works on paper, photographs, and extensive archival material—provide the occasion for an expansive survey of one of the twentieth century’s most influential artists. The host institutions have been given free curatorial rein. 


			
			
			
	
			
					View of the 2026 exhibition “Brancusi” at the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin.
									Photo David von Becker. ©Succession Brancusi/VG Bild-Kunst
	



	Designed by Mies van der Rohe, Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie offers up the ideal venue for Brancusi’s crisp distillations of form, at least in theory. Interrupted by just four load-bearing columns in its main gallery space, the open plan practically begs for vertical interventions by Brancusi—one of the twentieth-century artists most in tune with van der Rohe’s consummately modernist, “Less is More” sobriety. 

	In practice, puzzling choices by curators Klaus Biesenbach and Maike Steinkamp rendered the experiment fraught in places. Conservation questions surely informed certain placements (glass vitrines, elevated platforms). Yet the setting of so many of the sculptures against the wall impeded the kind of looking the works demand. Bird in Space (1923) was made to look decidedly agoraphobic. One had to crane one’s neck (almost impossibly) to get a glimpse of the maquette which Brancusi made for the lintel of the Kiss gate (1935–37)—part of his war memorial in Târgu Jiu, Romania. 
	


			
			
			
	
			
					View of the 2026 exhibition “Brancusi” at the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin.
									Photo David von Becker. ©Succession Brancusi/VG Bild-Kunst
	



	The exhibition did lend welcome attention to the full gamut of Brancusi’s media and formats.  Present in photographic form, his 1918 Endless Column (part of the same Târgu Jiu complex) forms just one of several arresting architectural designs. These also offer oblique insight into the relation of his sculptures to their carved bases, miniature structures in their own right, after all, which often rival their objects for attention.   

	Yet some of the show’s rather obtuse groupings (“Portraits,” “Animals,” “Bird in Space”) precluded more nuanced considerations, which might have included materials, questions of primitivism, gender, folk culture vs. high modernism, or any number of less literal taxonomies. One section bore the title “The Ambiguity of Form.” Perhaps no modernist artist proved less equivocal regarding form than Brancusi (save perhaps Mondrian). His sculptures evince a lapidary certainty even in their weird, seductive lyricisms.

	The elemental spareness of eggs and bones forms the metaphorical (and literal) touchstones of Brancusi’s series of resting heads (Sleep, Head of a Sleeping Child, The Newborn, etc.) and stylized “portraits” (Nancy Cunard, Eileen Lane, Princess X). The phallic arc of the latter sculpture—which caused a rumpus upon its debut at the 1920 Salon des Indépendants—exemplifies Brancusi’s conciliation of incongruous elements: lithe female corporeality and swollen male member; the mythical Leda and the Zeus-cum-swan who ravishes her; a young bird and the egg which birthed it.
	


			
			
			
	
			
					View of the 2026 exhibition “Brancusi” at the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin. 
									Photo David von Becker. ©Succession Brancusi/VG Bild-Kunst
	



	CHRISTIE’S PR VIGNETTE is not the first rendezvous between Brancusi’s legacy and something of the beau monde, as it were. A short film shot by Man Ray around 1930 on view herereveals Lee Miller running her hand over the smooth neck of Princess X. Rather than Miller’s budding career as a photographer, it is her fame as a model which seems the point here. The rhyme between her graceful form and the sculpture’s anatomy underscores the clip’s unmistakably erotic frisson.  

	Brancusi’s body of work has likewise informed the design of Balenciaga dresses, Rick Owens boots, and jewelry by the Tokyo-based Ambush firm—or, at least, it has informed their respective publicity campaigns. Among the objects that the Bulgari designer Mary Katrantzou wishes she had made, the T Magazine reported recently, figures Brancusi’s Sleeping Muse (1910) for its managing to be “devoid of any intricacy.” 

	Intricacy need not present itself as such, of course. In that paradox lies the beguiling complexity of Brancusi’s work, which he often carved frommarble, wood, or limestone without recourse to the molding process (what sculptors call taille directe). Even his cast bronze sculptures quite literally reflect the obsessive acts of polishing or the application of patina to which he submitted them. The modest volumes of Sleeping Muse, or Danaïde, or Bird in Space belie an intricate and iterative labor, which in turn erased its own traces. 
	

	Attesting to his labor is an ovoid pavilion at the exhibition’s center recreating Brancusi’s studio, chock-a-block with his myriad tools and flanked by walls on both sides bearing letters, photographs, and archival items. From postcard exchanges with Fernand Léger and Blaise Cendrars to documents of his artistic formation in Romania, the material puts intellectual, professional, and personal flesh back on the bareboned laconicism of his sculptures.

	The fundamentally subtractive ethos of Brancusi’s vision gave rise to a phenomenon that one journalist deemed—with a seemingly unironic oxymoron—a “minimalism glut” taking over contemporary American culture. Detailed by Kyle Chayka in his book The Longing for Less (2020), that sensibility informs everything from the penchant for sleek, streamlined appliances to “decluttered” lifestyle practices (at least, it must be said, among those with the means to dispense with luxury trappings or material excess to begin with).  


			
			
			
	
			
					View of the 2026 exhibition “Brancusi” at the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin. 
									Photo David von Becker. ©Succession Brancusi/VG Bild-Kunst
	



	Brancusi’s sensibility echoes elsewhere than high-end design or social trends, to be sure. The German curator Nicolaus Schafhausen explored the “The Brancusi Effect” on the work of several artists and architects in 2014. His exhibition and book notably featured the German architect Jürgen Mayer H. and industrial designer Konstantin Grcic; the sculptor and video artist Shahrayr Nashat; and a global group of conceptual artists including Sofia Hultén, André Cadere, and Saâdane Afif. The range in itself attests to the varied ramifications of Brancusi’s corpus. 
	

	Though it now sits behind glass at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, it was Brancusi’s marble Sculpture for the Blind (c. 1920) that shifted sculpture’s invitation to the viewer from the rational, metaphysical plane of sight to the embodied experience of touch. While not as frenziedly as Naum Gabo’s Kinetic Construction (Standing Wave) (1919–20), the buffed Leda (1926) was once mounted atop a spinning metal disc—footage of which appears in Berlin, along with a new rotating display.

	One wall text claims that Brancusi aimed to depict his animals in motion. Yet while Leda’s table may spin, her form remains singularly still. Seal reveals only the slightest of obliques, while the wooden Turtle (1940)—like The Cock (1924), Maiastra (1910), and other creatures—retain a hieraticism just shy of symmetry. The stateliness of Brancusi’s sculptures is never reducible to some platonic idea of nature, however. Even in the fixedness of their forms—their sententious certitude—a single work may conflate the erotic and the machinic, the vernacular and the archetypal, the abstract and the practical.

	First shipped stateside in 1926 for a retrospective organized by the photographer Edward Steichen, Bird in Space was initially charged with an import tax upon “manufactured metal objects.” Only a subsequent court case and deposition by the artist famously restored the work’s aesthetic pedigree on US soil, undoing its putative tax status as a “tool.” From Steichen (a keen photographer of the sculptor’s work) to Duchamp (a close confidant) to the collector John Quinn, Brancusi’s American reception inflects his oeuvre with a particular set of cultural, professional, and interpretive contingencies. What MoMA will make of these a hundred years later remains to be seen.
